subject: Object-Oriented Programming
summary: Object-oriented programming is the discipline of welding data and the rules that guard it into classes, so invariants live in one place instead of every call site. Interviews test it because it is the shared vocabulary of design: the four pillars, SOLID, and pattern names are how engineers communicate architecture in review and on whiteboards — and because Python's object model (MRO, dunders, properties, class attributes) separates people who write Python from people who understand it. This subject rewards a specific study method: for every mechanism, first learn the failure it prevents (the procedural mess, the isinstance ladder, the leaked inheritance API), then run the fix in code. Every section here carries runnable Python with asserts — execute them, break them, and re-derive the output before your interview. Then drill the traps section: mutable defaults, class-attribute shadowing, and super()'s real routing are the three questions most likely to appear verbatim.

sections.title: 1. Classes, Objects, and Why OOP Exists
sections.content:
Before you memorize the four pillars, understand the disease OOP was invented to cure. In procedural code, data and the rules that protect it live apart. Your account balance sits in a dict; the rule "balance can never go negative" sits in a function in some other file; and every one of the 30 places that touch the dict must remember to call that function. One caller forgets, and your data is corrupt with no error, no stack trace, nothing. The bug surfaces three weeks later in a report, far from the line that caused it.

A class is the fix: a blueprint that welds data (attributes) and the rules that guard it (methods) into one unit. An object is one concrete instance stamped out from that blueprint, with its own copy of the data. The class decides which operations exist; if `deposit()` and `withdraw()` are the only doors into `_balance`, then the invariant (a condition that must always be true, like "balance >= 0") is enforced in exactly two places instead of thirty.

```ascii
PROCEDURAL                              OBJECT-ORIENTED
data:  acct = {"balance": 0}            +------------------------+
rules: deposit(), withdraw()            |        Account         |
       ...scattered across files        |------------------------|
                                        | _balance   (guarded)   |
ANY code can write:                     |------------------------|
acct["balance"] = -999   <- no error    | deposit()   the ONLY   |
                                        | withdraw()  doors in   |
                                        +------------------------+
```

The runnable proof below shows both versions. The dict version accepts a corrupt write silently; the class version raises. When the interviewer asks "why OOP?", they are testing whether you can name the concrete failure mode of the alternative — say "invariants enforced in one place instead of every call site", not "code reuse". Reuse is a side benefit; protection of state is the core sale. One more term you will use constantly: `self` is the explicit reference to "this particular object" — Python passes it as the first argument to every method, which is why `a.deposit(100)` is really `Account.deposit(a, 100)`.
sections.code:
# The procedural version: data and behavior live apart.
def make_account(owner):
    return {"owner": owner, "balance": 0}

def deposit(acct, amount):
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
    acct["balance"] += amount

acct = make_account("Priya")
deposit(acct, 100)
# Nothing stops any caller from bypassing the rule:
acct["balance"] = -999           # corrupted, silently
assert acct["balance"] == -999   # the dict cannot defend itself

# The OOP version: data and its rules travel together.
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner):
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = 0        # leading underscore = internal, do not touch

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += amount

    @property
    def balance(self):           # read allowed, write blocked
        return self._balance

a = Account("Priya")
a.deposit(100)
assert a.balance == 100
assert Account.deposit is not None and a.deposit(1) is None  # bound method works

try:
    a.balance = -999             # property has no setter -> AttributeError
    raised = False
except AttributeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "the class version defends its invariant"

# a.deposit(100) is sugar for Account.deposit(a, 100) — self is explicit
b = Account("Rahul")
Account.deposit(b, 50)
assert b.balance == 50
print("OK: the class kept balance valid; the dict could not")

sections.title: 2. Pillar 1 — Encapsulation with Properties
sections.content:
Encapsulation is the discipline of hiding an object's internal state behind a controlled interface, so the object can guarantee its own invariants. The problem it solves: if any code anywhere can write `temp.celsius = -500`, then "temperature is physically valid" is not a guarantee, it is a hope.

Java solves this with `private` fields plus getter/setter methods. Python deliberately has no `private` keyword; it uses convention plus one mechanism. The convention: a single leading underscore (`_balance`) means "internal — touch this and you own the breakage". The mechanism: `@property`, a decorator (a function that wraps another function to change its behavior) that makes a method look like a plain attribute. Callers write `t.celsius = 100` — clean attribute syntax — but your setter code runs on every write and can validate, log, or recompute.

This is the killer feature interviewers probe: in Python you start with a plain public attribute and upgrade it to a property later without changing a single caller, because the access syntax is identical. In Java you must write getters up front "just in case". So the Pythonic rule is: public attribute first, property only when you actually need validation or a computed value.

```ascii
caller writes  t.celsius = 100
                    |
                    v
        @celsius.setter runs        <- validation gate
        reject if < -273.15
                    |
                    v
        self._celsius = 100          <- real storage, underscore-private
```

Double underscore (`__pin`) triggers name mangling: Python rewrites the attribute to `_ClassName__pin` at compile time. Its purpose is preventing accidental name clashes between a parent class and a subclass that both use `__x` — it is a collision guard, not security. As the code proves, the mangled name is still reachable. If an interviewer asks "does Python have private variables?", the strong answer is: no true privacy; underscore is a social contract, name mangling is clash protection, and properties are how you enforce invariants without breaking callers.

sections.title: 3. Pillar 2 — Inheritance and the MRO
sections.content:
Inheritance solves duplication of behavior: when `Car` and `Truck` share 90% of their logic, you lift the shared part into `Vehicle` and each subclass states only its differences. The subclass "is-a" parent: everywhere a `Vehicle` is accepted, a `Car` must work (that promise is the Liskov principle, section 9).

Single inheritance is easy. The interview questions live in multiple inheritance: if `D` inherits from both `B` and `C`, and both define `who()`, which one runs? Python answers with the MRO — Method Resolution Order, the exact linear sequence of classes Python searches for an attribute. It is computed by the C3 linearization algorithm, which guarantees two properties: every child is searched before its parents, and the left-to-right order of the base-class list is preserved. You can always inspect it: `D.mro()` or `D.__mro__`.

```ascii
        A                D(B, C)
       / \
      B   C     D.mro() == [D, B, C, A, object]
       \ /
        D       lookup of d.who(): try D, then B -> found, stop
```

This "diamond" shape (two paths from D up to A) is the classic trap. Naive depth-first search would visit A before C, so C's overrides would be silently skipped; C3 visits A exactly once, after both B and C.

Now the part most candidates get wrong: `super()` does not mean "my parent". It means "the NEXT class after me in the MRO of the actual runtime object". In the code below, `Left.greet` calls `super().greet()` and lands in `Right` — a class Left has never heard of — because the object is a `Child` and Child's MRO is [Child, Left, Right, Base]. This is called cooperative multiple inheritance: every class calls `super()`, and the MRO threads one call through the entire chain, hitting each class exactly once. It is exactly how mixins (small classes that add one feature and expect to be combined) work in Django and DRF. If C3 cannot build a consistent order — for example `class X(A, B)` alongside `class Y(B, A)` and then a class inheriting both — Python refuses to create the class and raises TypeError at class-definition time, not at call time.

sections.title: 4. Pillar 3 — Polymorphism: Duck Typing and abc
sections.content:
Polymorphism means one call site, many behaviors: `publish(doc)` works whether `doc` renders JSON or XML, and adding a YAML renderer next month requires zero changes to `publish`. The problem it solves is the if/elif ladder — `if kind == "json": ... elif kind == "xml": ...` — which every new type forces you to reopen and re-test.

Python gives you two roads to polymorphism, and interviewers love asking you to compare them.

Road one: duck typing — "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". No declared interface at all: `publish` calls `doc.render()`, and any object with a `render` method qualifies, regardless of its class tree. This is idiomatic Python and covers most day-to-day code. Its cost: the check happens at call time. Pass an object without `render`, and you get AttributeError deep inside the call, possibly in production.

Road two: `abc` — the abstract base class module. An ABC declares required methods with `@abstractmethod`; any subclass missing one cannot even be instantiated — the failure moves from "deep at call time" to "loudly at object creation". Use an ABC when the interface is a real contract between teams, when there are many implementations to keep honest, or when a half-implemented subclass shipping to production would be expensive.

```ascii
duck typing                    abc contract
publish(doc) --> doc.render()  Notifier(ABC)  <- declares send()
  any object with render()        ^       ^
  fails LATE (call time)       Email     Sms
                               fails EARLY (instantiation time)
```

There is a middle road worth naming in interviews: `typing.Protocol` (structural typing, Python 3.8+) lets a static type checker like mypy verify duck typing before you even run the program — you declare the shape, but classes never have to inherit from it. Strong answer shape: "duck typing by default, Protocol when I want static checking without coupling, ABC when I need runtime enforcement and a shared implementation to inherit."

sections.title: 5. Pillar 4 — Abstraction and Template Methods
sections.content:
Abstraction is often confused with encapsulation, so separate them cleanly: encapsulation hides an object's internal STATE (you cannot write `_balance` directly); abstraction hides the internal PROCESS (you call `pay(100)` and never learn whether Stripe or Razorpay ran underneath, or what retry logic fired). Encapsulation protects data; abstraction reduces what the caller must understand.

The problem abstraction solves is cognitive load and coupling. If checkout code knows the six steps of charging a card through Stripe, then checkout must change whenever Stripe's steps change, and whoever reads checkout must understand payments. Put a `PaymentProcessor` abstraction between them, and checkout knows one verb: `pay(amount)`. Swapping providers becomes a one-line change at the point where the concrete class is created.

In Python the tool is the same `abc` module from the previous section, but used with a second idea: the template method pattern. The abstract base class implements the shared skeleton as a concrete method (`pay`: validate amount, then charge, later maybe log and retry), and declares only the variable step (`charge`) as abstract. Subclasses fill in exactly one hole. The skeleton is written once, tested once, and cannot drift between providers.

```ascii
caller --> processor.pay(100)          PaymentProcessor (ABC)
              |                        +--------------------------+
              v                        | pay(amount)     concrete |  <- skeleton
        validate amount                | charge(amount)  ABSTRACT |  <- the hole
              |                        +--------------------------+
              v                            ^              ^
        self.charge(100) ----------> StripeProcessor  RazorpayProcessor
                                     fills the hole   fills the hole
```

Interview framing: when asked "abstraction vs encapsulation", weak candidates give dictionary definitions; strong candidates give this split — state versus process — and then name the enforcement tools: properties and underscore for encapsulation, ABCs and template methods for abstraction. Note what the code proves: instantiating the ABC raises TypeError, and so does instantiating a subclass that forgot `charge`. The contract has teeth at object-creation time, which is the whole point of writing it down.

sections.title: 6. Composition over Inheritance
sections.content:
"Favor composition over inheritance" is the single most quoted design rule in interviews, so know exactly what each word buys you. Inheritance is "is-a": `Stack(list)` claims a stack IS a list. Composition is "has-a": `Stack` HAS a list inside, hidden as `_items`. The difference sounds cosmetic. It is not — it decides what your public API promises forever.

When you inherit, you inherit everything: `Stack(list)` publicly exposes all 40+ list methods — `insert`, `remove`, `sort`, slicing. Your class claims to be a stack (a LIFO container: last in, first out), but any caller can run `s.insert(0, 99)` and break LIFO with no error. Worse, once code in the wild depends on those leaked methods, you cannot remove them: the accident became the contract. This is how inheritance "rots": the subclass's real interface is its own methods PLUS every method of every ancestor, and it grows every time any ancestor grows. A parent adding one method silently changes every child's API.

```ascii
INHERITANCE (is-a)                  COMPOSITION (has-a)
      list                          Stack
       ^                            +----------------+
       |                            | _items: list   |  list lives INSIDE,
  Stack(list)                       +----------------+  invisible outside
  API = push, pop                   | push()  pop()  |
        + 40 leaked list methods    +----------------+
  s.insert(0, 99) breaks LIFO       API = exactly 3 things you chose
```

With composition, the wrapper starts with an empty public API and you add only what belongs. The inner list can later become a `collections.deque` or a linked list without any caller noticing — the implementation is swappable because it was never exposed. The cost is honest too: you write small forwarding methods (`__len__` delegating to `len(self._items)`), a few lines of boilerplate per operation you expose.

So when IS inheritance right? When all four hold: the relationship is truly is-a; you want to be substitutable everywhere the parent is accepted (Liskov, section 9); you want to inherit implementation, not only interface; and the parent was designed to be subclassed (documented hook points, like `abc` classes or framework base classes). Real ratio in application code: composition wins the large majority of the time; inheritance earns its place mostly for ABC contracts and framework extension points. Interview line that lands well: "inheritance is the strongest coupling my language offers, so it is the last tool I reach for, not the first."

sections.title: 7. SOLID Part 1 — S, O, L
sections.content:
SOLID is five principles about one enemy: change. Every letter answers "when requirements change, how much existing code must I edit and re-test?" Interviewers rarely want definitions — they want a violation you have seen and the refactor that fixes it. This section covers the first three letters with runnable violations and fixes.

S — Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have one reason to change. The violation is the God class: a `Report` that computes totals, formats text, AND writes files. Three stakeholders — finance changing the formula, design changing the layout, ops changing storage — all edit the same class, stepping on each other in code review and merge conflicts. The fix in the code splits it into `ReportData`, `ReportText`, `ReportSaver`: each has exactly one axis of change. Warning for interviews: SRP does not mean "one method per class" or "as small as possible" — it means one REASON to change, judged by who asks for the change.

O — Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification. The violation smell is the isinstance/elif ladder: `total_area` checking `isinstance(s, Circle)... elif isinstance(s, Square)...`. Every new shape reopens tested code, and forgetting a branch fails at runtime. The fix: each shape carries its own `area()`; adding `Triangle` means adding a class — the summing function never changes again.

L — Liskov Substitution Principle: any subclass must be usable wherever its parent is promised, without the caller knowing the difference. The famous violation is `Square(Rectangle)`. Mathematically a square is a rectangle; behaviorally it is not, because Rectangle promises "set_w changes width only", and Square must break that promise to stay square.

```ascii
stretch(r): r.set_w(4); r.set_h(5); expects area == 20
Rectangle(1,1) -> 4 * 5 = 20   promise kept
Square(1)      -> set_h(5) also changed w -> 5 * 5 = 25   promise broken
```

The code demonstrates the broken promise with asserts. The professional fix is to stop pretending: make Square NOT inherit Rectangle — either both derive from an immutable `Shape` with only `area()`, or Square stands alone. LSP is why "is-a in English" is not enough; the test is "does the subclass honor every behavioral promise of the parent?"
sections.code:
# --- S: split by reason-to-change ---
class ReportData:                        # changes when the FORMULA changes
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows
    def total(self): return sum(self.rows)

class ReportText:                        # changes when the LAYOUT changes
    def render(self, data): return f"TOTAL={data.total()}"

class ReportSaver:                       # changes when STORAGE changes
    def save(self, text, sink): sink.append(text)

sink = []
ReportSaver().save(ReportText().render(ReportData([1, 2, 3])), sink)
assert sink == ["TOTAL=6"]

# --- O: add a class, never edit the ladder ---
import math
class Circle:
    def __init__(self, r): self.r = r
    def area(self): return math.pi * self.r ** 2
class Sq:
    def __init__(self, s): self.s = s
    def area(self): return self.s ** 2

def total_area(shapes):                  # closed: never edited again
    return sum(s.area() for s in shapes)

assert abs(total_area([Circle(1), Sq(2)]) - (math.pi + 4)) < 1e-9

class Triangle:                          # extension: NEW code only
    def __init__(self, b, h): self.b, self.h = b, h
    def area(self): return self.b * self.h / 2
assert abs(total_area([Triangle(4, 3)]) - 6) < 1e-9

# --- L: Square(Rectangle) breaks the parent's promise ---
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w, self.h = w, h
    def set_w(self, w): self.w = w       # promise: width only
    def set_h(self, h): self.h = h       # promise: height only
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

class Square(Rectangle):                 # the classic LSP mistake
    def __init__(self, side): super().__init__(side, side)
    def set_w(self, w): self.w = self.h = w
    def set_h(self, h): self.w = self.h = h

def stretch(rect):                       # written against Rectangle's promises
    rect.set_w(4); rect.set_h(5)
    return rect.area()

assert stretch(Rectangle(1, 1)) == 20    # promise kept
assert stretch(Square(1)) == 25          # promise BROKEN: caller gets 25, not 20
print("SOLID S/O/L OK — and the LSP break is visible: 25 != 20")

sections.title: 8. SOLID Part 2 — I, D
sections.content:
I — Interface Segregation Principle: no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. The violation: one fat `Machine` interface with `print_doc()`, `scan()`, and `fax()`. An old printer that only prints must still implement `scan` — usually as `raise NotImplementedError`, which is a landmine: the type system says "I can scan" while runtime says boom. Fat interfaces also create phantom coupling: change the signature of `fax()` and every printer recompiles/retests, including ones that never fax. The fix is splitting into small role interfaces — `Printer`, `Scanner` — and letting each class implement exactly the roles it truly supports. A multifunction device implements several; a basic device implements one and never lies.

D — Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level policy should depend on abstractions, not on concrete details — and the concrete object should be handed in from outside (dependency injection: passing a dependency through the constructor instead of building it inside). The violation looks innocent: `UserService.__init__` does `self.db = PostgresClient()`. Now the service cannot be unit tested without a real Postgres, cannot switch storage without editing service code, and secretly imports a driver. The fix in the code: `UserService` accepts any object satisfying the `Store` ABC; production passes a Postgres-backed store, tests pass `MemoryStore`. High-level logic is now testable in milliseconds and storage is swappable at one location — the composition root (the single place at app startup where concrete objects are created and wired together).

```ascii
BEFORE (violates D)              AFTER (inverted)
UserService --> PostgresClient   UserService --> Store (ABC)
  hard-wired inside                              ^         ^
  untestable without a DB              PostgresStore   MemoryStore
                                       (production)      (tests)
```

Interview framing: DIP is the principle behind every mock you have ever injected in a test — say that out loud and the interviewer knows you have actually used it, not memorized it. And a caution that reads as seniority: applying all of SOLID everywhere produces over-abstracted lasagna code (ten one-line classes to print a string). The principles are levers you pull WHERE change is expected — around vendors, storage, and formats — not a religion applied to every helper function.

sections.title: 9. Dunder Methods — the Python Object Protocol
sections.content:
Every operator and builtin in Python is a method call in disguise. `a + b` runs `a.__add__(b)`; `len(x)` runs `x.__len__()`; `x in box` runs `box.__contains__(x)`; `for item in box` asks for `box.__iter__()`. These double-underscore methods ("dunders") form the object protocol — the set of hooks that let YOUR classes plug into the language's own syntax. The problem they solve: without them, a `Money` type forces callers into `m1.add(m2).equals(m3)` Java-speak; with them, `m1 + m2 == m3` reads like arithmetic because it IS arithmetic.

The dunders every interview touches: `__init__` (initializer — note: NOT the constructor; `__new__` creates the object, `__init__` fills it in). `__repr__` (unambiguous developer string — aim for valid Python that could rebuild the object; `__str__` is the user-facing one and falls back to `__repr__` if missing). `__eq__` (equality by value — without it, `==` falls back to identity, comparing memory addresses). `__hash__` — and here is the trap: defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, making your objects unusable in sets and as dict keys until you define `__hash__` too, over the same fields as `__eq__` so equal objects hash equal.

```ascii
a + b:
  1. try type(a).__add__(a, b)
       returns NotImplemented?  -> 2. try type(b).__radd__(b, a)
       returns NotImplemented?  -> 3. raise TypeError
```

`NotImplemented` is the polite refusal: returning it (never raising it) from `__add__` tells Python "I do not know this operand type — ask the other object". That double dispatch is why `2 * my_vector` can work even though `int` knows nothing about vectors: int refuses, Python tries `my_vector.__rmul__`.

Also load-bearing: `__lt__` makes objects sortable; `__len__` and `__iter__` make containers loop-able and give truthiness (empty means falsy); `__enter__`/`__exit__` power `with`; `__slots__` fixes the attribute set, saving memory and blocking typo-attributes. When the interviewer asks "how would you make your class work with sorted() / sets / +", they are testing whether you know Python's syntax is a protocol you can implement, not magic reserved for builtins. Mention `@dataclass` at the end — it writes `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__` for you — and you signal practical experience.

(Refinement: when the right operand is a proper subclass of the left and overrides the reflected method, its __radd__ runs before the parent’s __add__.)

sections.title: 10. Patterns I — Singleton (and Why It Is Disliked) and Factory
sections.content:
A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem — vocabulary first, code second. When a teammate says "make it a Strategy", that one word transmits a whole structure. Interviews test patterns for exactly that reason: shared vocabulary is how seniors communicate design. Start with the two most asked.

Singleton guarantees a class has exactly one instance with a global access point. The Python route: override `__new__` (the actual constructor that allocates the object, running before `__init__`) to return a cached instance. The honest use cases are few — a config object, a connection pool, a logger.

Now the part interviewers really want: why is Singleton the most disliked pattern? Because it is global mutable state wearing an OOP costume. Concretely: (1) hidden coupling — any function anywhere can reach `Config()` and mutate it, so data flows through your program along edges no function signature reveals; (2) test pollution — the code below PROVES it: test_one sets a flag, and test_two, which never touched it, sees the leftover state, so tests pass alone and fail together depending on order; (3) it hard-wires a dependency, the exact thing Dependency Inversion (section 8) tells you to invert. The senior answer: "I create ONE instance at the composition root and inject it — one-ness by discipline, not by class design." Also know: modules in Python are natural singletons (imported once, cached in sys.modules), so `config.py` with module-level values is often the pragmatic version.

Factory moves the "which concrete class?" decision out of client code. The violation smell is `if ext == "json": parser = JsonParser() elif ext == "csv": ...` copy-pasted in five places.

```ascii
client --> parser_for("data.json") --> registry lookup --> JsonParser()
           ONE place decides           {"json": JsonParser,
           clients stay clean           "csv":  CsvParser}
```

The registry-dict version shown below is the Pythonic factory: adding a format touches one dict entry, unknown formats fail fast with a clear error, and — combined with Open/Closed — client code never reopens. When asked "where have you used Factory?", point at any place a string from config or a filename extension picks an implementation.

sections.title: 11. Patterns II — Strategy, Observer, Decorator
sections.content:
Three more patterns that come up constantly, each solving a specific coupling problem.

Strategy: you have one job (compute a price) and several interchangeable algorithms for it (regular, festival discount, member pricing). The naive version is an if/elif ladder inside `Checkout`, which reopens tested code for every new promotion — an Open/Closed violation. Strategy extracts the algorithm into its own object (or, idiomatically in Python, a plain function, because functions are first-class objects you can pass around) and injects it into the context. Adding a promotion becomes writing one new function. If your interviewer uses Java examples with a `PricingStrategy` interface, mention that Python collapses the ceremony: a callable is the strategy.

Observer: an object (the publisher, or "subject") must tell an unknown, growing set of other objects (subscribers) that something happened — order placed, so email, analytics, and inventory all react. The naive version has `place_order` directly calling all three, meaning the order module imports and knows every downstream team's code. Observer inverts it: subscribers register callbacks (functions handed over to be called later) with an event bus; the publisher fires the event knowing nobody. This is the in-process seed of every event-driven system you will meet — Django signals, GUI onClick handlers, Kafka consumers are the same shape at different scales.

```ascii
Strategy: Checkout(pricing_fn) -> swap the algorithm, context untouched
Observer: bus.publish("order_placed", 42)
             |--> log subscriber      (publisher knows NONE of them)
             |--> email subscriber
Decorator: WithSugar(WithMilk(Coffee())).cost() -> 40 + 10 + 5 = 55
           wrap object in object, same interface, stacked add-ons
```

Decorator (the pattern): add behavior to an object without subclassing, by wrapping it in another object that exposes the SAME interface and delegates, adding its bit before or after. Why not inheritance? Combinations explode: Coffee with milk, with sugar, with both — subclassing needs a class per combination (2^n classes for n add-ons); wrapping composes at runtime in any order. Python's `@decorator` syntax is the identical idea applied to functions — `audited(pay)` wraps `pay` in a same-shaped callable that logs, then delegates. Saying "the @ syntax IS the Decorator pattern for functions" in an interview shows you see the concept, not the ceremony.

sections.title: 12. Reading UML Class Diagrams
sections.content:
UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagrams appear in low-level-design interviews as the whiteboard shorthand for "show me your classes and how they relate". You do not need the full standard — you need to read and draw four relationship arrows and one box format, because interviewers sketch these while talking and expect you to follow.

The box: three stacked compartments — class name, attributes, methods. Visibility markers: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected. `+start()` is a public method; `- engine` is a private attribute.

The four arrows, ordered from weakest coupling to strongest:

```ascii
Driver .......> Vehicle      dependency: "uses briefly" (a parameter,
                             a local variable). Dashed arrow.
Car o------- Wheel          aggregation: has-a, but the part outlives
                             the whole (wheels survive the car). HOLLOW diamond.
Car *------- Engine          composition: has-a, part DIES with the whole
                             (engine has no life outside). FILLED diamond.
Car -------|> Vehicle        inheritance: is-a. HOLLOW TRIANGLE pointing
                             at the PARENT.
```

A full diagram for the code below:

```ascii
+------------------+          +---------------+
|     Vehicle      | *------- |    Engine     |
|------------------|  has-a   |---------------|
| - engine         |          | + start()     |
|------------------|          +---------------+
| + start()        |
+------------------+
         ^
        /_\   hollow triangle = inheritance
         |
+------------------+          +---------------+
|       Car        | <........|    Driver     |
|------------------|  uses    |---------------|
| + wheels: int    |          | + drive(v)    |
+------------------+          +---------------+
```

Mapping to Python: inheritance is `class Car(Vehicle)`; composition and aggregation are both "attribute holding another object", differing only in who controls the part's lifetime (composition typically constructs the part inside `__init__` or fully owns it; aggregation receives an object that others also hold); dependency is a method parameter and nothing stored. Two traps interviewers check: the triangle points AT the parent (candidates draw it backwards under pressure), and multiplicity labels — `1`, `0..1`, `1..*` written at line ends — read like "one Car has 4 Wheels" (`4` near Wheel). When handed a diagram, read it aloud in coupling order: inheritance first (it constrains everything), then composition, then dependencies. That narration alone signals you have done design reviews before.
sections.code:
# The diagram from this section, translated line-by-line into Python
class Engine:
    def start(self): return "vroom"

class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, engine):
        self.engine = engine               # has-a (diamond edge)
    def start(self):
        return self.engine.start()         # delegate to the part

class Car(Vehicle):                        # is-a (hollow triangle edge)
    wheels = 4

class Driver:
    def drive(self, vehicle):              # dependency (dashed edge):
        return vehicle.start()             # parameter only, nothing stored

assert issubclass(Car, Vehicle)            # the triangle, checked at runtime
car = Car(Engine())
assert isinstance(car, Vehicle)
assert car.start() == "vroom"              # composition delegates
assert Driver().drive(car) == "vroom"      # dependency: uses, does not keep
assert Car.wheels == 4

# Aggregation vs composition is about lifetime, not syntax:
shared_engine = Engine()                   # part exists independently...
v1, v2 = Vehicle(shared_engine), Vehicle(shared_engine)
assert v1.engine is v2.engine              # ...and is shared: aggregation
assert not hasattr(Driver(), "vehicle")    # dependency stored nothing
print("UML mapping OK")

sections.title: 13. Interview Traps — Mutable Defaults, Class Attrs, super()
sections.content:
Three Python-specific traps show up in interviews because each one separates "writes Python" from "understands Python's object model". All three are demonstrated live in the code.

Trap 1 — mutable default arguments. `def add(item, bucket=[])` looks innocent. The catch: default values are evaluated ONCE, at `def` time, and stored on the function object itself (visible at `add.__defaults__`). Every call that omits `bucket` shares that one list, so items from the first call leak into the second. The idiom: default to `None`, create the list inside. When asked "why does Python do this?", the answer is that `def` is an executable statement, not a declaration — the defaults are computed when the function object is built, and re-evaluating them per call would need a rule for WHEN (fresh copy? deep copy?) that Python refuses to guess.

Trap 2 — class attributes vs instance attributes. A class attribute (`members = []` in the class body) is stored once on the class and shared by every instance. Attribute LOOKUP falls through: instance dict first, then class. Attribute ASSIGNMENT never falls through: `obj.x = 1` always writes to the instance. That asymmetry creates two opposite surprises. Mutation (`t1.members.append(...)`) walks up to the shared class list — every instance sees the change. Assignment-flavored code (`c.count += 1`) READS the class value 0 but WRITES an instance attribute 1, silently shadowing (hiding by sitting in front of) the class attribute, which stays 0.

```ascii
lookup  c.count:  instance dict {}        -> miss -> class dict {count: 0} -> 0
write   c.count = 0 + 1:  instance dict {count: 1}   class dict UNCHANGED
after:  c.count -> 1 (instance shadows)   Counter.count -> 0
```

Rule of thumb: class attributes are for constants shared by design (`wheels = 4`); anything mutable per object belongs in `__init__` as `self.x`.

Trap 3 — `super()` in multiple inheritance. Covered mechanically in section 3, here as a trap: candidates believe `super()` inside `B` calls "B's parent A". False when the runtime object's MRO says otherwise: for `D(B, C)`, the chain inside B's method routes to C next. Practical consequences interviewers listen for: in cooperative hierarchies, every `__init__` should call `super().__init__()` (even classes whose textual parent is `object`) and pass along `**kwargs`, or the chain breaks in the middle; and you never hard-code the parent name (`A.setup(self)`) because that freezes the routing the MRO is supposed to control.

interviewQA.q: Why does OOP exist? What concrete problem does it solve over procedural code?
interviewQA.a: Procedural code separates data from the rules that protect it. The balance lives in a dict; the rule 'never negative' lives in a function elsewhere; every one of the N call sites must remember to go through that function. One direct write like acct['balance'] = -999 corrupts state silently, and the bug surfaces far from its cause. A class welds data and its guarding methods into one unit, so an invariant (a condition that must always hold) is enforced at two doors — deposit and withdraw — instead of thirty call sites. The compiler-level benefit: you change the internal representation without touching callers, because they only ever used the methods. Reuse and modeling 'real-world objects' are side benefits; the core sale is state protection and a smaller blast radius for change. A strong answer names the failure mode of the alternative, not a dictionary definition.
followUps: When is procedural code the better choice?
How would you refactor a 2,000-line procedural script toward classes incrementally?
What is an invariant, and where exactly does a class enforce it?

interviewQA.q: Explain the four pillars of OOP with one Python mechanism for each.
interviewQA.a: Encapsulation: hide internal state behind a controlled interface — in Python, underscore-prefixed attributes plus @property setters that validate every write, so 'balance is never negative' is enforceable, not hoped for. Inheritance: share behavior through an is-a relationship — class Car(Vehicle), with the MRO deciding lookup order when hierarchies get wide. Polymorphism: one call site, many behaviors — publish(doc) calls doc.render() and works for any object with that method (duck typing), or against an abc contract when you want the failure at instantiation instead of call time. Abstraction: hide process, not just state — a PaymentProcessor ABC exposes pay() while the Stripe-vs-Razorpay details stay invisible to the caller. The differentiator interviewers listen for: encapsulation hides STATE, abstraction hides PROCESS. Give the Python tool for each pillar and you have proven you use them, not just define them.
followUps: Which pillar do you use most in day-to-day work, and why?
Can you have polymorphism without inheritance in Python?
How do properties make Python encapsulation different from Java's getters?

interviewQA.q: What is the MRO, and how does Python resolve methods in a diamond hierarchy?
interviewQA.a: The MRO — Method Resolution Order — is the exact linear sequence of classes Python searches when you access an attribute, computed by the C3 linearization algorithm and inspectable via ClassName.mro(). C3 guarantees: every child appears before its parents, and the left-to-right order of the base-class list is preserved. In the diamond — D(B, C) with both inheriting A — the MRO is [D, B, C, A, object], so A is visited exactly once, after BOTH B and C. Naive depth-first search would visit A before C and silently skip C's overrides; C3 exists to prevent exactly that. If no order can satisfy all constraints (X(A, B) alongside Y(B, A), then Z(X, Y)), Python raises TypeError at class-definition time rather than guessing. Bonus point: super() means 'next in the MRO of the runtime object', not 'my parent' — which is why cooperative mixin chains work at all.
followUps: What happens to the MRO if you swap the base order to D(C, B)?
Why does C3 reject some hierarchies at class-creation time instead of runtime?
How do Django-style mixins depend on the MRO?

interviewQA.q: How does super() actually behave in multiple inheritance? Many people think it calls the parent.
interviewQA.a: super() returns a proxy that continues the method lookup from the NEXT class after the current one in the MRO of the actual runtime object — not the textual parent. Concretely: with D(B, C) where both B and C inherit A, calling super().setup() inside B's method routes to C when the object is a D, even though B's code never mentions C. The same line inside B routes to A when the object is a plain B. This is cooperative multiple inheritance: if every class in the hierarchy calls super(), one initial call threads through every class exactly once, in MRO order. Practical rules that signal experience: always call super().__init__() in cooperative hierarchies (even when the textual parent is object), forward **kwargs so the chain can pass arguments through, and never hard-code the parent (A.setup(self)) because that freezes routing the MRO should control and breaks any future mixin insertion.
followUps: Why should __init__ methods in a mixin hierarchy accept and forward **kwargs?
What breaks if one class in the chain forgets to call super()?
When would you deliberately call a parent class explicitly instead of super()?

interviewQA.q: Duck typing versus abstract base classes — when do you use which?
interviewQA.a: Duck typing: call doc.render() and accept any object that has the method, no declared relationship needed. It is idiomatic Python, zero ceremony, and right for most internal code. Its cost: a wrong object fails with AttributeError at call time, possibly deep in production. An ABC moves that failure earlier — a subclass missing an @abstractmethod cannot even be instantiated, so a half-implemented notifier dies at object creation, not after messages were dropped. Choose ABCs when the interface is a contract between teams, when there are many implementations to keep honest, or when the ABC also carries shared skeleton code (template method). The middle road worth naming: typing.Protocol gives structural typing — mypy verifies the duck's shape statically, with no inheritance coupling at all. Interview-grade summary: duck typing by default, Protocol when I want static checks without coupling, ABC when I need runtime enforcement plus shared implementation.
followUps: What does @abstractmethod actually do mechanically at instantiation time?
How is typing.Protocol different from an ABC at runtime?
Can an ABC have concrete methods, and why would it?

interviewQA.q: Python has no private keyword. So how do you do encapsulation seriously?
interviewQA.a: Three layers. Convention: one leading underscore (_balance) marks an attribute internal — tools and reviewers treat access as a contract violation, though nothing enforces it. Mechanism: @property turns attribute access into method calls, so t.celsius = 100 runs a validating setter — invariants are enforced on every write while callers keep plain attribute syntax, and you can upgrade a public attribute to a property later without changing any caller. Name mangling: double underscore (__pin) rewrites to _ClassName__pin at compile time — its real purpose is preventing accidental name clashes between a base class and subclass using the same private name; it is a collision guard, not security, and remains reachable deliberately. The philosophy answer that lands: Python chooses 'we are all consenting adults' — enforcement through review and properties where it matters, instead of compiler walls everywhere. If someone truly needs to break in for debugging, the language allows it, and that trade is intentional.
followUps: When would you convert a plain attribute into a property in real code?
What problem does name mangling actually solve — show a collision scenario?
How does __slots__ interact with encapsulation and memory?

interviewQA.q: Explain 'composition over inheritance'. Why does inheritance rot?
interviewQA.a: Inheritance is is-a and imports the parent's ENTIRE public API into your class forever: Stack(list) exposes insert, sort, and slicing, so any caller can break LIFO with s.insert(0, 99), and once wild code depends on leaked methods you cannot remove them — the accident became the contract. It also couples you upward: when a parent adds a method, every child's API silently grows. That is the rot. Composition is has-a: Stack holds a hidden _items list and exposes only push, pop, and len — an API you chose, defended by the class. The inner list can become a deque with zero caller changes because it was never visible. The cost is small forwarding methods. Inheritance still earns its place when all four hold: true is-a, full substitutability (Liskov), you want implementation not just interface, and the parent was designed for subclassing (ABCs, framework base classes). One-liner for interviews: inheritance is the strongest coupling the language offers, so it is my last tool, not my first.
followUps: Show the same feature built both ways — what changes in the public API?
When is inheriting from list or dict actually acceptable?
How does the Decorator pattern relate to composition?

interviewQA.q: State the Liskov Substitution Principle and give the classic violation.
interviewQA.a: LSP: any subclass must be usable wherever the parent type is promised, without the caller detecting the difference — the subclass must honor every behavioral promise of the parent, not merely match method signatures. Classic violation: Square(Rectangle). Rectangle promises set_w changes width ONLY; a square must keep sides equal, so Square's set_w also changes height. Code written against Rectangle's promise — set_w(4); set_h(5); expect area 20 — gets 25 from a Square. Nothing crashed; an assumption silently broke, which is worse. The lesson: 'is-a in English' is not the test; 'honors the behavioral contract' is. Fixes: do not inherit — make both derive from an immutable Shape exposing only area(), or keep Square independent. Other LSP smells to name: overrides that raise NotImplementedError (see Interface Segregation), overrides that strengthen preconditions (parent accepted any int, child demands positive), and overrides returning different types. LSP is the principle behind 'subclass, but never surprise the caller'.
followUps: Why does making Rectangle immutable dissolve the Square problem?
How does an override that raises NotImplementedError violate LSP?
How would you test a hierarchy for LSP compliance?

interviewQA.q: Walk through SOLID — one violation and one fix per letter.
interviewQA.a: S, single responsibility: a Report class computing totals, formatting text, and saving files has three stakeholders editing one class; split into ReportData, ReportText, ReportSaver — one reason to change each. O, open/closed: total_area built on isinstance/elif reopens tested code per new shape; give each shape area() and the summing loop never changes again. L, Liskov: Square(Rectangle) breaks 'set_w changes width only' — callers expecting area 20 get 25; stop inheriting, derive both from an immutable Shape. I, interface segregation: a fat Machine interface forces an old printer to fake scan() with NotImplementedError; split into Printer and Scanner roles so each class implements only what it honestly supports. D, dependency inversion: UserService constructing PostgresClient inside is untestable and welded to a vendor; depend on a Store ABC, inject MemoryStore in tests and the real store at the composition root. Close with the caution: SOLID applies where change is expected — over-applying it everywhere yields ten one-line classes to print a string.
followUps: Which SOLID principle do you see violated most in real codebases?
How do O and D work together when adding a new payment provider?
What does over-applied SOLID look like, concretely?

interviewQA.q: What is dependency injection, and why do interviewers care about it so much?
interviewQA.a: Dependency injection is passing a component its dependencies from outside (usually through the constructor) instead of letting it construct them internally. UserService(store) receives any object satisfying the Store contract; it never runs PostgresClient() itself. Interviewers care because DI is where design theory becomes daily practice: it is the mechanical realization of Dependency Inversion, and it is the reason unit tests can exist — you inject a MemoryStore or a mock and test business logic in milliseconds with no database, no network, no docker. It also creates a composition root: one startup location where all concrete objects are created and wired, so swapping a vendor is a one-line change there instead of a hunt through the codebase. Without DI you get hidden coupling — dependencies invisible in signatures, discovered only when the test suite demands a live Postgres. Saying 'DI is why my mocks work' proves you have used the principle, not memorized it. Frameworks can automate the wiring, but plain constructor-passing in Python covers most real needs.
followUps: What is a composition root, and what goes wrong without one?
Constructor injection versus passing dependencies per method call — trade-offs?
Does Python need a DI framework the way Java uses Spring?

interviewQA.q: Why is Singleton called an anti-pattern, and what do you do instead?
interviewQA.a: Singleton guarantees one instance with global access — and that second half is the poison: it is global mutable state in OOP costume. Three concrete harms. Hidden coupling: any function can reach Config() and mutate it, so data flows along edges no signature reveals — reading a function's parameters no longer tells you what it depends on. Test pollution: test A sets a flag on the singleton, test B silently observes it; the suite passes alone and fails in a different order — the definition of flaky. Hard-wired dependency: callers construct Config() themselves, the exact thing Dependency Inversion says to avoid, making substitution for tests impossible without monkeypatching. The professional alternative: create ONE instance at the composition root and inject it everywhere — one-ness by discipline, plus testability. Python-specific point worth adding: modules are natural singletons (cached in sys.modules after first import), so a config.py with module-level values is often the pragmatic version — with the same global-state cautions.
followUps: When is a singleton genuinely acceptable?
How does __new__-based Singleton behave across threads?
Why are Python modules described as natural singletons?

interviewQA.q: Explain the Strategy pattern and how Python makes it lighter than in Java.
interviewQA.a: Strategy solves 'one job, several interchangeable algorithms': computing a price under regular, festival, and member rules. The naive form is an if/elif ladder inside Checkout, which reopens tested code for every new promotion — an Open/Closed violation — and makes each algorithm untestable in isolation. Strategy extracts each algorithm into its own unit and injects it: Checkout(pricing) calls self.pricing(base) and never knows which rule it holds. Adding a promotion is writing one new strategy; the context is closed. In Java this needs a PricingStrategy interface plus one class per algorithm. Python collapses the ceremony because functions are first-class objects: a lambda or plain function IS the strategy, and a dict mapping names to functions IS the strategy registry. Use a class-based strategy only when the algorithm carries its own state or several related methods. Where it shows up in real code: sorted(key=...), pricing rules, retry/backoff policies, serialization format choices. Naming those makes it obvious you have used it.
followUps: Strategy versus a plain if/elif — at what point does the pattern pay for itself?
How does Strategy interact with the Open/Closed principle?
When would a strategy need to be a class rather than a function?

interviewQA.q: Describe the Observer pattern and where it appears in systems you have used.
interviewQA.a: Observer decouples 'something happened' from 'who reacts'. The publisher (subject) keeps a list of subscribers — callbacks registered in advance — and on an event calls each with the payload, knowing nothing about what they do. Problem solved: without it, place_order directly calls email, analytics, and inventory code, so the order module imports every downstream team and must be edited each time a new reaction appears. With a bus, subscribers register themselves; the publisher's code never changes — Open/Closed applied to events. Where it appears: GUI onClick handlers, Django signals (post_save), webhooks, and message queues like Kafka — the same shape at increasing scale, with the bus moving out of process. Trade-offs a strong candidate names: execution order among subscribers is usually unspecified, one failing subscriber can break the loop unless the bus isolates errors, debugging is harder because the call chain is invisible in the code, and in long-lived processes forgotten subscribers cause leaks (why weak references appear in real event systems).
followUps: How do you stop one failing subscriber from breaking the others?
What is the memory-leak risk in Observer, and how do weak references help?
How does in-process Observer differ from a message queue like Kafka?

interviewQA.q: What are dunder methods, and what exactly happens when Python evaluates a + b?
interviewQA.a: Dunders (double-underscore methods) are the hooks that let your classes plug into the language's own syntax — the object protocol. len(x) runs x.__len__(); x in c runs c.__contains__(x); for loops call __iter__. For a + b the resolution is double dispatch: first type(a).__add__(a, b); if that returns the sentinel NotImplemented (returned, never raised — it means 'I do not recognize this operand'), Python tries type(b).__radd__(b, a); if both refuse, TypeError. That refusal chain is why 2 * my_vector can work although int knows nothing about vectors — int declines, Python asks the vector's __rmul__. The trap worth volunteering: defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, so your objects become unusable in sets and as dict keys until you define __hash__ over the same fields, keeping 'equal implies same hash' true. Also distinguish __repr__ (unambiguous, developer-facing, ideally rebuildable) from __str__ (user-facing, falls back to __repr__), and __new__ (creates the object) from __init__ (fills it in). One refinement: if the right operand’s type is a proper subclass of the left’s and overrides the reflected method, Python tries __radd__ FIRST — that is what lets a subclass customise mixed arithmetic with its parent.
followUps: Why must __hash__ agree with __eq__, and what breaks in a dict if it does not?
Difference between NotImplemented and NotImplementedError?
Which dunders does @dataclass generate for you?

interviewQA.q: Explain the mutable default argument bug and why Python behaves that way.
interviewQA.a: def add(item, bucket=[]) stores ONE list on the function object at def time — visible at add.__defaults__ — and every call that omits bucket shares it. So add(1) returns [1], and a later independent-looking add(2) returns [1, 2]: state leaked across calls. The bug hides well because it only fires on the default path and only after the second call, so it passes shallow testing and surfaces in production as mysterious accumulation. The fix idiom: default to None and create the list inside the body — a fresh object per call. Why Python works this way: def is an executable statement, not a declaration; the default expressions are evaluated exactly once, when the function object is constructed. Re-evaluating per call would require the language to guess when and how to copy (shallow? deep? re-run arbitrary expressions with side effects?), and Python refuses to guess. Same trap applies to dict, set, and any mutable default — and the same once-only evaluation is why datetime.now() as a default freezes at import time.
followUps: Why is datetime.now() as a default argument a bug, and what is the fix?
When is a mutable default used deliberately, e.g., as a cache?
How do linters and type checkers catch this class of bug?

interviewQA.q: Class attributes versus instance attributes — explain the shadowing trap.
interviewQA.a: A class attribute lives once on the class and is shared by all instances; an instance attribute lives in that object's own __dict__. Lookup is asymmetric with assignment, and that asymmetry is the trap. Lookup falls through: reading obj.x checks the instance dict first, then the class. Assignment never falls through: obj.x = value ALWAYS writes to the instance. Two opposite surprises follow. With a mutable class attribute (members = [] in the class body), t1.members.append('asha') mutates the one shared list, so every instance sees it — usually an accidental global. With c.count += 1 where count = 0 is on the class, Python reads the class value 0, computes 1, and writes an INSTANCE attribute — silently shadowing (sitting in front of) the class attribute, which remains 0. So mutation shares; assignment shadows. Rule: class attributes for constants shared by design (wheels = 4); anything mutable and per-object belongs in __init__ as self.x. Diagnosis tool: c.__dict__ shows the shadow; type(c).__dict__ shows the original.
followUps: Is c.count += 1 shadowing ever the behavior you actually want?
How do class attributes interact with inheritance lookup order?
Where do methods themselves live — instance or class dict?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between __new__ and __init__?
interviewQA.a: __new__ is the constructor: a static-like method on the class that ALLOCATES and returns the new object; __init__ is the initializer: it receives that already-created object as self and fills in attributes, returning None. The sequence when you call Config(): Python runs Config.__new__(Config), and if the returned object is an instance of Config, then runs __init__ on it. You override __new__ only when you must control creation itself: Singleton (return a cached instance instead of a new one), subclassing immutable types like int, str, or tuple (by __init__ time an immutable's value is already fixed, so customization must happen in __new__), and interning/caching patterns that reuse instances. A subtlety that impresses: if __new__ returns an object that is NOT an instance of the class, __init__ is skipped entirely. And the Singleton gotcha: with the standard pattern, __init__ still runs on EVERY Config() call, re-initializing the shared instance — which is why the cached-instance setup belongs inside __new__ or must be guarded.
followUps: Why can't you customize the value of a subclassed int in __init__?
In the __new__-based Singleton, how do you stop __init__ from re-running?
When does __init__ get skipped entirely?

interviewQA.q: Abstraction versus encapsulation — most candidates blur them. Separate them precisely.
interviewQA.a: Encapsulation hides an object's internal STATE: callers cannot write _balance directly; every write passes a validating gate (property setter), so the object can guarantee its invariants. Its tools in Python: underscore convention, @property, name mangling for clash protection. Abstraction hides the internal PROCESS: callers invoke processor.pay(100) and never learn whether Stripe or Razorpay ran, how many retries fired, or what the six charging steps are. Its tools: ABCs defining WHAT without HOW, and template methods holding the shared skeleton while subclasses fill one hole. The crisp separation: encapsulation protects data from invalid modification; abstraction protects callers from irrelevant knowledge. They compose naturally — an Account encapsulates _balance while its deposit() abstracts away ledger entries and audit logging. Test yourself: if removing it would let callers corrupt state, it was encapsulation; if removing it would force callers to understand more steps, it was abstraction. Giving that state-versus-process split with the tools for each is the answer that ends the question.
followUps: Give one class from your current job that does both — which part is which?
Can you have abstraction without inheritance or ABCs in Python?
How does a template method serve abstraction?

flashcards.front: What core problem does a class solve that a dict plus functions cannot?
flashcards.back: It welds data and its guarding methods into one unit, so invariants are enforced at the few method doors instead of every call site. A dict accepts acct['balance'] = -999 silently; a class with a property raises.

flashcards.front: What is self in Python?
flashcards.back: The explicit reference to the current instance. a.deposit(100) is sugar for Account.deposit(a, 100) — Python passes the object as the first argument to every method.

flashcards.front: Encapsulation vs abstraction in one line each?
flashcards.back: Encapsulation hides STATE (no direct writes to _balance; properties validate). Abstraction hides PROCESS (call pay(); never learn the vendor's steps). State vs process is the separation interviewers want.

flashcards.front: What does @property buy you over a plain attribute?
flashcards.back: Attribute syntax for callers (t.celsius = 100) while your getter/setter code runs on every access — validation, computed values, logging. You can upgrade a public attribute to a property later without changing any caller.

flashcards.front: What does double underscore (__pin) actually do?
flashcards.back: Name mangling: rewritten to _ClassName__pin at compile time. Purpose is preventing parent/child attribute name collisions — a clash guard, not security. Still reachable via the mangled name.

flashcards.front: What is the MRO and which algorithm computes it?
flashcards.back: Method Resolution Order: the exact linear class sequence searched for attributes, computed by C3 linearization. Guarantees child before parents and preserves left-to-right base order. Inspect with ClassName.mro().

flashcards.front: MRO of D(B, C) where B and C both inherit A?
flashcards.back: [D, B, C, A, object]. A is visited once, AFTER both B and C — that ordering is why the diamond problem does not skip C's overrides the way naive depth-first search would.

flashcards.front: What does super() really refer to?
flashcards.back: The NEXT class in the MRO of the runtime object — not the textual parent. Inside B, super() can route to sibling C when the object is a D(B, C). Cooperative calls thread once through the whole MRO.

flashcards.front: When does Python reject a class hierarchy with TypeError before any call?
flashcards.back: When C3 cannot build a consistent MRO — e.g., X(A, B) and Y(B, A), then Z(X, Y). The contradiction is detected at class-definition time, not at method-call time.

flashcards.front: Duck typing — definition and its cost?
flashcards.back: Any object with the right methods qualifies, no declared type needed ('walks like a duck'). Cost: a wrong object fails with AttributeError late, at call time, possibly deep in production.

flashcards.front: What does @abstractmethod enforce, and when?
flashcards.back: A subclass that fails to implement the method cannot be instantiated — TypeError at object creation. Moves the failure from call time to construction time. The ABC itself is also uninstantiable.

flashcards.front: typing.Protocol vs ABC — the one-line difference?
flashcards.back: Protocol is structural: classes match by shape, checked statically by mypy, no inheritance required. ABC is nominal: subclasses register/inherit explicitly and enforcement happens at runtime instantiation.

flashcards.front: What is a template method?
flashcards.back: A concrete method on an ABC holding the shared skeleton (validate, then charge, then log) that calls abstract hook methods subclasses must fill. Skeleton written and tested once; only the variable step differs per subclass.

flashcards.front: Why does Stack(list) rot as a design?
flashcards.back: Inheritance exposes the parent's whole API: insert/sort/slicing leak, so callers can break LIFO. Once external code uses leaked methods, they are frozen contract. Composition (has-a hidden list) exposes only push/pop/len.

flashcards.front: Four conditions under which inheritance is the right tool?
flashcards.back: True is-a relationship; full substitutability (Liskov holds); you want implementation reuse, not only an interface; and the parent was designed for subclassing (ABC or framework base class with documented hooks).

flashcards.front: State the Single Responsibility Principle precisely.
flashcards.back: One class, ONE REASON TO CHANGE — judged by stakeholders, not method count. Report computing + formatting + saving serves three stakeholders; split so finance, design, and ops each edit a different class.

flashcards.front: The code smell that signals an Open/Closed violation?
flashcards.back: An isinstance/elif ladder over types. Every new type reopens tested code. Fix: each type carries its own method (shape.area()); extension becomes adding a class, the ladder function is never edited again.

flashcards.front: Why does Square(Rectangle) violate Liskov?
flashcards.back: Rectangle promises set_w changes width only. Square must keep sides equal, so set_h also changes width: code expecting set_w(4); set_h(5) -> area 20 gets 25. Signatures match; the behavioral promise broke.

flashcards.front: The Interface Segregation smell inside a class body?
flashcards.back: A method stubbed with raise NotImplementedError to satisfy a fat interface (old printer forced to 'implement' scan). Fix: split into small role interfaces so every class implements only what it honestly supports.

flashcards.front: Dependency Inversion in one sentence, plus its everyday payoff?
flashcards.back: High-level code depends on an abstraction (Store ABC) and receives the concrete object from outside. Payoff: inject MemoryStore in tests — business logic tested in milliseconds with no database. DI is why mocks work.

flashcards.front: What is a composition root?
flashcards.back: The single startup location where concrete objects are created and wired together (UserService(PostgresStore())). Swapping a vendor is a one-line change there instead of edits scattered through the codebase.

flashcards.front: Why is Singleton disliked? Name the three harms.
flashcards.back: It is global mutable state: (1) hidden coupling — any code can reach and mutate it, invisible in signatures; (2) test pollution — order-dependent flaky tests; (3) hard-wired dependency, blocking substitution. Prefer one instance injected from the composition root.

flashcards.front: What is the natural singleton built into Python?
flashcards.back: The module. Imported once, cached in sys.modules; every importer sees the same object. A config.py with module-level values is the pragmatic singleton — with the same global-state cautions.

flashcards.front: Factory pattern — the problem and the Pythonic shape?
flashcards.back: Problem: 'which concrete class?' if/elif ladders copy-pasted across clients. Shape: one registry dict {ext: cls} plus a lookup function; adding a format is one entry, unknown inputs fail fast with a clear error.

flashcards.front: Strategy pattern in idiomatic Python?
flashcards.back: The interchangeable algorithm is a first-class function injected into the context: Checkout(pricing) calls self.pricing(base). New promotion = new function; no interface class needed unless the strategy carries state.

flashcards.front: Observer pattern — who knows whom?
flashcards.back: Subscribers register callbacks with the publisher/bus; the publisher fires events knowing nothing about reactions. Adding a reaction touches only the new subscriber. Same shape as Django signals, GUI handlers, Kafka.

flashcards.front: How does the Decorator pattern beat subclassing for add-ons?
flashcards.back: Wrappers share the interface and delegate, adding their bit: WithSugar(WithMilk(Coffee())). n add-ons compose at runtime in any combination; subclassing would need up to 2^n classes. Python's @ syntax is the same idea for functions.

flashcards.front: Resolution order for a + b?
flashcards.back: type(a).__add__(a, b); if it returns NotImplemented, try type(b).__radd__(b, a); if both refuse, TypeError. Return NotImplemented, never raise it — it is the 'ask the other operand' sentinel.

flashcards.front: You define __eq__ and your objects stop working in sets. Why?
flashcards.back: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None (unhashable). Define __hash__ over the same fields so equal objects hash equal — then sets and dict keys work correctly again.

flashcards.front: __repr__ vs __str__?
flashcards.back: __repr__: unambiguous, developer-facing, ideally rebuildable Python like Money(5, 'INR'); used in containers and debuggers. __str__: user-facing display; falls back to __repr__ when missing. Always implement __repr__ first.

flashcards.front: __new__ vs __init__?
flashcards.back: __new__ allocates and returns the object (the real constructor) — override for Singleton or subclassing immutables like int/str, whose value is fixed before __init__. __init__ initializes the already-created object and returns None.

flashcards.front: Why does def f(x, bucket=[]) leak state between calls?
flashcards.back: Defaults are evaluated ONCE at def time and stored on the function (f.__defaults__); every default-path call shares that one list. Fix: default None, create the list inside the body.

flashcards.front: Class attribute trap: what do mutation and assignment each do?
flashcards.back: Mutation (t1.members.append) reaches the ONE shared class list — all instances see it. Assignment (c.count += 1) reads class 0 but writes an instance attr 1, shadowing the class attr, which stays 0. Mutation shares; assignment shadows.

flashcards.front: In UML, which way does the inheritance triangle point, and what do the diamonds mean?
flashcards.back: Hollow triangle points AT the parent. Filled diamond = composition (part dies with the whole); hollow diamond = aggregation (part outlives the whole); dashed arrow = dependency (uses briefly, stores nothing).

flashcards.front: What does __slots__ do and what does it catch?
flashcards.back: Fixes the allowed attribute names, removing the per-instance __dict__: less memory per object, and typo-attributes (m.amout = 5) raise AttributeError instead of silently creating a new attribute.

flashcards.front: Aggregation vs composition — the actual test, since Python syntax looks identical?
flashcards.back: Lifetime and ownership. Composition: the whole owns/constructs the part; the part dies with it (engine built inside the car). Aggregation: the part exists independently and may be shared (one engine object held by two vehicles).
